title: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq Futures Mixed After Fed Holds Rates Steady: GOOG, GOOGL, IOVA, MSFT, NOW In Focus - Stocktwits
content: U.S. stock futures were mixed overnight late Wednesday after the Federal Reserve held interest rates steady at a target range of 3.75%-4.00% in its October policy meeting. As of 10:33 p.m. EDT, Dow futures gained 0.32%, while the S&P 500 futures were down 0.50% and Nasdaq-100 futures fell 1.60%. On Wednesday, U.S. benchmark indexes closed higher. The Nasdaq Composite closed up 0.27%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.19%, while the S&P 500 climbed 0.28%. Markets were largely focused on the Federal Reserve’s policy decision on Wednesday. The central bank held rates steady, passing with a 10-2 vote, and largely in line with expectations. “Inflation remains elevated,” the Fed said in the statement. “The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability.” However, market participants were split on whether this was the right decision amid rising inflation and soaring energy prices. DoubleLine Capital CEO Jeffrey Gundlach said the Fed should raise rates, pointing to the two-year Treasury yield and a steepening yield curve. Others, including University of Michigan economist Betsey Stevenson and BlackRock’s Rick Rieder, said waiting is justified. Mohamed El-Erian, Chief Economic Advisor at Allianz, said in a post on X, “Quite a few of those now calling for rate hikes because inflation has exceeded target for over five years supported a series of rate cuts last year—when inflation had already been above target for four years. This isn't an argument against a policy response; inflation demands one. But there remains far too much focus on monetary policy and far too little on tools better suited to the task, including  fiscal consolidation.” Meanwhile, results from Alphabet Inc. (GOOG, GOOGL) were also in focus in the extended trading hours. The Google parent’s shares slid nearly 10% in the overnight session after third-quarter (Q3) adjusted earnings per share and revenue missed Street expectations. Negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion and a full-year capital expenditures forecast of $195 billion to $205 billion also weighed on sentiment. Other artificial intelligence stocks slipped in sympathy, with Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) falling about 1% at the time of writing, while Micron Technology Inc. (MU) fell nearly 4%. Chip stocks closed higher on Wednesday before Alphabet’s results. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) closed up 2%, while the Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X Shares (SOXL) surged more than 6%. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) gained nearly 2%. Markets will now turn their attention to the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index report. The first reading of third-quarter GDP and weekly jobless claims are also due. Meanwhile, on the geopolitical front, Iran and the U.S. offer conflicting accounts of negotiations for a peace deal. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran remains in close contact with mediators on proposals to implement its seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, U.S. President Donald Trump denied reports that he had asked Vice President JD Vance to initiate peace talks with Iran, saying the contact instead concerned Tehran’s need for medical supplies. Brent crude futures were trading at $114.35 a barrel, down nearly 1%, while WTI crude futures traded 1.19% lower at $101.56 per barrel. Alphabet Inc. (GOOG, GOOGL): Shares of the company were on the retail radar after it posted disappointing Q3 results, sending the stock lower overnight. Iovance Biotherapeutics Inc. (IOVA): The stock jumped more than 11% overnight as an upcoming lung-cancer data presentation is fueling optimism about its cell therapy’s potential beyond melanoma. Microsoft Corp. (MSFT): Shares gained more than 3% after-hours following the software maker’s first-quarter results, which surpassed Wall Street expectations. ServiceNow Inc. (NOW): The stock plunged nearly 19% in extended trading hours after the company’s Q3 results fell below Wall Street expectations, weighed down by its acquisition of cybersecurity firm Armis. Among ETFs tracking benchmark indexes, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) and the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) were trending lower overnight, while the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) edged higher. Meanwhile, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield was trading at 4.984%, while the 30-year yield was 5.31%. The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT) was up 0.68% amid ‘bearish’ sentiment. Asian markets opened mixed on Thursday. South Korea's KOSPI and China’s SSE Composite were down at the time of writing, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 and Australian stocks ticked higher at the open. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Comments posted here will also appear on symbol pages. Shares of Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SPCX) slipped 1% overnight heading into Wednesday as T-Mobile CEO Srini Gopalan doubled down on his rejection of a mobile virtual network operator (MVNO) arrangement with SpaceX, saying he sees “no room” for a deal in either consumer wireless or physical and edge AI. SPCX stock fell over 2% on Wednesday to $145.23, bringing its weekly losses to nearly 2%. “But the answer to the MVNO is I see no room for an MVNO with SpaceX, either on the consumer side or on the physical and Edge AI side,” Gopalan said on T-Mobile’s third-quarter (Q3) earnings call. An MVNO sells wireless service using wholesale access to another carrier’s network. Such a deal could support a SpaceX-branded mobile offering, while the company develops its own terrestrial infrastructure. Gopalan said T-Mobile’s criteria remain unchanged: additional customers, new distribution channels or capabilities. “The way we think about it is, does an MVNO give us access to incremental TAM? Does it give us access to new distribution channels? Does it give us incremental capability of any sort?” he said. When asked whether an edge-computing partnership could offer an alternative to SpaceX building its own network, Gopalan pointed to T-Mobile’s standalone 5G investments and preparations for 6G. “We see ourselves in the lead in terms of those capabilities, and we see no space for an MVNO here because what additional capabilities does it give us? Why does it change our ability to compete?” he said. T-Mobile is already working with Amazon Web Services on Kinetic Edge, combining its wireless network and distributed computing infrastructure with AWS cloud and AI services. Gopalan said SpaceX’s shifting strategy was making the company harder to define. “It's hard to refer to them now as a satellite provider or a satellite provider that is going to build terrestrial,” he said. He also questioned the value of pairing satellite broadband with T-Mobile’s fixed wireless access (FWA), which delivers internet over cellular networks. “We've got a great product in FWA, and really in many ways, except for some deep rural parts, satellite is an inferior version of FWA with even more constraints in terms of things like what is the size of the beam, right?” Gopalan said. “I don't see the synergy there between FWA and satellite.” Two-thirds of T-Mobile’s FWA customers are in dense urban areas, he said, where the company still sees plenty of room to grow using spare network capacity. Meanwhile, Gopalan left the door open to other business with SpaceX, including satellite resale through T-Satellite. “If we're talking about SpaceX as a customer or us being a customer of them, that's a purely commercial agreement,” he said. “If it's a complementary product, I'm very happy to look at a resale arrangement, which is exactly what T-Satellite was, which gets built into it.” He also drew a clear line between the approach and a broader wholesale mobile deal. “But an MVNO is a wholly different thing, so I hope that clarifies where our head's at on MVNOs and more broadly, satellite.” The stance is consistent with his earlier comments. Gopalan questioned a Starlink MVNO at a Morgan Stanley conference in March and again on T-Mobile’s April earnings call, when he said satellite usage was lower than expected and mostly concentrated in national parks. He later cited May data showing T-Satellite accounted for just 0.0002% of total network usage. SpaceX is gathering spectrum and exploring tower access to build a mobile network combining satellites with ground infrastructure. Earlier this month, Grain Management agreed to sell its nationwide 800 MHz spectrum portfolio to SpaceX, pending FCC approval and other closing conditions. SpaceX is also reportedly seeking access to at least 80,000 U.S. cell sites, with Crown Castle among the companies in talks. However, established carriers have pushed back. T-Mobile's parent, Deutsche Telekom, warned earlier this month that a SpaceX MVNO could undercut carriers’ retail pricing. AT&T CEO John Stankey also pointed to incumbents’ extensive spectrum holdings and indoor coverage infrastructure. Verizon CEO Dan Schulman said: “I see absolutely no benefit whatsoever to extending an MVNO deal to any satellite provider.” He estimated that a competitive ground network would take at least four to six years to build and cost $300 billion to $500 billion over seven or eight years. Shares of key enterprise software markers pulled back in overnight trading late Wednesday after quarterly results from ServiceNow (NOW) and Fortinet (FTNT) failed to meet investors’ lofty expectations, with further pressure from Alphabet (GOOGL) reporting weakness in its core Search and Advertising business. Palo Alto Networks (PANW) networks declined 5.5% in sympathy selling after peer cybersecurity firm Fortinet’s stock dropped over 25%. Fortinet’s product revenue grew significantly slower in the latest quarter than in the previous one, while some analysts noted that its beat on billings and revenue was smaller than desired. Product revenue rose 37% in the third quarter, compared to 52% in Q2. Salesforce (CRM) dropped 4.7%, while Intuit (INTU) and Adobe (ADBE) shed about 2% each, following ServiceNow’s report. The iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV), a proxy for the software-as-a-service (SaaS) sector, fell 3%. ServiceNow, the flagbearer of Saas rebound in recent months, reported mixed Q3 results, with its pipeline of new AI deals overshadowed by an earnings miss and evidence of slowing contract growth ahead. Adjusted earnings in the quarter were $1 per share, below the $1.17 analysts had expected. Revenue and remaining performance obligations each rose 20.5% to  $4.13 billion and  $13.65 billion, beating expectations. However, an 18.5% RPO growth forecast for Q4 came in below a Bloomberg estimate of 19%. Alphabet’s report added to the selling pressure. GOOGL stock dropped nearly 10% after Google Services revenue, largely driven by advertising, came in at $96.3 billion, below analysts’ expectations of $98.5 billion, The Wall Street Journal reported, overshadowing a doubling of sales in its cloud unit. After plunging to multi-year lows earlier this year on fears that AI would reduce demand for niche enterprise software, SaaS stocks strengthened in recent months, partly due to strong Q2 earnings and investors rotating out of red-hot chip stocks. The latest move suggests concerns about a slowdown have not entirely faded. Retail sentiment on the sector was mixed. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment was ‘bearish’ for CRM, ‘neutral’ for IGV, ‘extremely bearish’ for INTU, and ‘extremely bullish’ for FTNT. The sentiment for NOW turned ‘extremely bullish’ from ‘neutral,’ while the sentiment for ADBE turned ‘bearish’ from ‘neutral.’ “$NOW $CRM $IGV haven’t touched software in months because the run just got too overstretched. They weren’t moving on fundamentals. It was simply an opposite to the chip trade. That officially ended tonight. Expect major downside the next few weeks,” said a trader. (WEN) stock is heading for its strongest weekly gain since June after the company said it will evaluate Nelson Peltz’s Trian-led investor group’s $ 7.35-per-share buyout offer, valuing the fast-food chain at roughly $1.43 billion. Retail traders are betting rival bidders could emerge, despite TD Cowen’s cautious outlook. Wendy’s stock edged 0.6% higher overnight Wednesday, after a 15% gain in regular session. The stock has gained 13% so far this week. On Wednesday, Wendy’s confirmed it received an unsolicited takeover offer from a group of investors seeking to acquire shares they do not already own. The investor group includes Trian Fund Management, Flynn Group, BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners. Wendy’s said a committee made up of independent board members will assess the offer. Nelson Peltz and Trian Partners together own more than 24% of Wendy’s, making them its largest shareholder. Peltz owns about 16% of the company, while Trian holds another 7.9%. The buyout speculation has been brewing since June. In August, Wendy’s reported second-quarter revenue of $571 million, up 1.7% year-on-year. Adjusted revenue came in at $443.15 million, below analysts’ $557.73 million expectation, according to Fiscal.ai. Earnings reached $0.18 per share, beating estimates of $0.16. U.S. same-store sales fell 7% as fewer customers visited its restaurants. CEO Bob Wright said the company was falling short on customer traffic, value and franchisee profitability. Wendy’s also dropped its 2026 financial forecast and slashed its dividend. TD Cowen reiterated a ‘Hold’ rating on WEN, noting that taking the fast-food chain private under Trian's umbrella offers the operational flexibility needed to execute a multi-year turnaround. The firm expects no competing offers to emerge given Trian's existing large ownership stake and deep operational ties to the company. On Monday, UBS lowered its price target for Wendy’s to $6.50 from $8 and kept a ‘Neutral’ rating, expecting sales and earnings to stay weak. The firm said Wendy’s plans to help franchise owners and attract more customers, but a lasting recovery could take time. Shares of Viking Therapeutics (VKTX) fell nearly 3% overnight late Wednesday after posting a wider-than-expected quarterly loss, while CEO Brian Lian’s outlook for an obesity-drug launch more than two years away also sparked retail backlash. VKTX stock rose nearly 2% to $25.36 on Wednesday, bringing its weekly gain to about 4% and putting it on track to end a four-week losing streak. Lian’s timeline came during a discussion of commercial preparations for VK2735, Viking’s experimental obesity treatment targeting the GLP-1 and GIP receptors. “We have a pretty solid commercial team, especially given that we're 2 and a half years out from potential launch,” he said on Wednesday’s earnings call. Viking is developing both injectable and tablet versions of VK2735 as it seeks to compete in an obesity-treatment market led by Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk. Lian said Viking has hired leaders in commercial operations, market access and medical affairs, and added staff in supply chain, technical operations, quality and compliance. Viking reported a third-quarter (Q3) loss of $1.55 per share, compared with the $1.06 loss analysts expected. Net loss more than doubled to $183.2 million from $90.8 million a year earlier. Research and development expenses rose to $166.8 million from $90 million as trial and manufacturing costs increased. General and administrative expenses climbed to $20.3 million from $8.6 million. Viking ended September with $960 million in cash, equivalents and short-term investments, up from $706 million at year-end. Stock and convertible-note offerings raised about $575 million before expenses during the quarter. “But I think as we think about cash, just company-wide, I think we'd see a usage of average of around $100 million per quarter,” CFO Greg Zante said. “But some quarters will be higher, some will be lower moving forward.” Viking has four Phase 3 trials underway. Both injectable Vanquish trials are fully enrolled and on track, with the first patients expected to enter extension studies in early 2027. The oral Sunrise program began earlier this month. “If successful, we believe these studies will position VK2735 as the first oral formulation of a dual GLP-1/GIP agonist to reach the market,” Lian said. When asked about tablet doses, he said Viking wanted fewer and smaller pills while protecting margins. “We also want to make sure that the program makes economic sense. We need to have sufficient gross margins to allow us to run a highly profitable enterprise,” he said. Less-frequent treatment is another part of Viking’s pitch. After 21 weeks of weekly injections in its earlier maintenance study, patients switched to every-other-week dosing retained 83%-97% of their initial weight loss over the next 12 weeks. Monthly cohorts retained 82%-90%, versus 61% for patients switched to placebo. However, a label for less-frequent dosing may come later, supported by the larger Vanquish extension studies. “But it seems more likely that the VANQUISH extension data would be sort of a standalone package that would be a supplement later. But again, too early to say definitively,” Lian said. A second maintenance study, including a switch from injections to daily tablets, is expected to report results in 2027. Viking also plans to start a 28-day multiple-dose study of its amylin drug VK3019 in the first quarter of 2027. Shares of Iovance Biotherapeutics (IOVA) jumped 12% in extended trading on Wednesday as an upcoming lung-cancer data presentation fueled optimism about its cell therapy’s potential beyond melanoma. IOVA stock rose nearly 2% Wednesday, bringing its weekly gain to 5% and putting it on track for a second straight week of gains. The company said it will share positive results for Lifileucel in previously treated advanced lung cancer on Thursday. The announcement comes after encouraging results in sarcoma and melanoma, adding to interest in how widely the treatment could be used. The trial tests one-time Lifileucel tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy in previously treated nonsquamous metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (mNSCLC). The company will also discuss precision-medicine opportunities for its TIL platform in lung cancer. At ESMO, it presented research examining tumor-reactive T-cell clones in patients who responded to Lifileucel. Lifileucel is already sold as Amtagvi for previously treated advanced melanoma. The lung-cancer announcement came just two days after Iovance reported early results in two soft tissue cancers: undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (UPS) and dedifferentiated liposarcoma (DDLPS). Four of the first eight evaluable patients had confirmed partial responses, giving the small pilot trial a 50% objective response rate. All four responses were ongoing at the Sept. 9 cutoff, lasting at least six weeks and at least 46 weeks. Patients had received between one and seven prior systemic treatments. Iovance said the safety findings were consistent with the Lifileucel treatment regimen in other cancers. “This level of durability provides meaningful time for patients with refractory UPS and DDLPS suffering from high disease burden, poor quality of life, and a lack of effective treatments, including no approved immunotherapy options,” said Lauren Banks, the trial’s principal investigator and a sarcoma medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. Iovance is now enrolling patients in its Phase 2 Saratoga registrational trial in the two sarcoma types. Lifileucel received FDA fast track designation for advanced UPS and DDLPS in the second quarter of 2026. The company’s recent updates also included final Phase 2 results, released last week, for Lifileucel combined with Pembrolizumab in previously untreated advanced melanoma. Of the 24 patients studied, 62.5% had a confirmed response, including 29.2% who achieved a complete response. Median overall survival had not been reached after a median study follow-up of 50.9 months. “About half of patients do not experience lasting benefit with frontline combination immunotherapy for advanced melanoma,” said trial investigator Andrew J.S. Furness. The results support Iovance’s ongoing Phase 3 Tilvance-301 study, which compares Lifileucel plus Pembrolizumab with Pembrolizumab alone. The trial will support approval for earlier use in advanced melanoma and serve as the confirmatory study for full U.S. approval of Amtagvi in previously treated advanced melanoma. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for IOVA jumped to ‘bullish’ from ‘neutral’ levels a day ago amid ‘normal’ message volume. One user said, “Personally, I was expecting the NSCLC data in December — but now we’re getting this update already tomorrow!” Another trader predicted a much bigger rally: “This stock is set to see an unprecedented, meteoric rise—this is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity that will never come around again” For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. title: CMB International Securities Remains a Buy on Microsoft (MSFT) - The Globe and Mail

title: S&P 500, Nasdaq Futures Dip As Weaker-Than-Expected Alphabet Earnings Reignite AI Spending Worries — GOOGL, MSFT, ORCL, NVDA, MRVL In Focus - Stocktwits
content: U.S. stock indices ended higher on Wednesday as the Federal Reserve’s decision to keep interest rates unchanged helped cool some inflation worries, while weak earnings from Alphabet led the Nasdaq 100 to drop after-hours. The S&P 500 ended Wednesday 0.3% higher, the Nasdaq 100 rose 0.5%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.2%. The Russell 2000, which tracks small-cap stocks, added 0.4%. Meanwhile, Nasdaq-100 futures lost 1.2%. S&P 500 futures declined 0.5%, while Dow Jones Industrial Average futures lost 17 points, or 0.03% at the time of writing. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) gained 0.6%, and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (DIA) rose 0.2%. Meanwhile, the Nasdaq-100 tracking Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) ended 0.5% higher on Wednesday. Meanwhile, the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) and the iShares Semiconductor ETF jumped about 2% each on Wednesday as gains in AMD, Micron Tech (MU) and Broadcom (AVGO). The broader Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT) rose 0.6%. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits for SPY improved to ‘neutral’ from ‘bearish’, while it remained in ‘bearish’ territory for DIA and QQQ. The Federal Reserve opted to keep its target interest rate steady on Wednesday, but financial markets focused on Chair Kevin Warsh's announcement of a structural shift in the frequency of future interest rate decisions. title: Can Microsoft Turn a Leaner Workforce and Record AI Spending Into Bigger Profits? - MarketBeat
content:
The shares, trading near $525 following the company's fiscal year 2027 Q1 results on Oct. 28, gave back their initial post-earnings gains. However, they're still up roughly 10% in 2026 and about 50% above their June 2026 low. In other words, Microsoft isn't offering buyouts because its business is shrinking; it's doing so from a position of financial strength. That’s the heart of the debate for investors. Does a leaner headcount point to fatter margins as AI does more of the work, or could substantial departures hint at trouble brewing beneath the AI boom? The bullish reading is that Microsoft could be shedding payroll from a position of strength, not because it's scrambling to plug a hole. Revenue in the most recent quarter rose almost 19% to more than $92 billion, operating income landed near $46 billion, and the operating margin held at roughly 50%, a touch higher than a year earlier. Operating expenses rose just 6%, far more slowly than that 19% jump in sales, and headcount had already edged down about 2% year over year as of June 2026, before this latest effort even landed. Layer the AI story on top, and the logic sharpens. Microsoft’s Azure platform grew revenue 48% last quarter, daily Copilot users jumped nearly 50% from the prior three months, and management says it’s wringing far more work out of the same computing power. If AI really does let Microsoft generate more revenue per employee, a leaner workforce paired with disciplined spending is exactly how margins could climb from here. Seen that way, the buyout offer is less a cost cut than a reallocation: dollars moving out of payroll and into the data centers Microsoft is betting its next decade on. The bearish reading starts with that same buildout. Microsoft spent roughly $45 billion on capital projects in a single quarter, expects to clear $50 billion in the next fiscal quarter, and has pointed to something near $170 billion for the calendar year. That’s a vast sum to commit before the AI revenue fully shows up, and it’s already biting: free cash flow fell 27% to $18.6 billion in the latest quarter as cash capital spending more than doubled. If infrastructure, depreciation, and energy costs outrun the money AI brings in, no amount of payroll trimming will paper over the gap. There are softer spots, too. Windows OEM and Devices revenue fell 22% in the most recent quarter, and the exit offer reportedly reached even some AI and Copilot teams, which could be seen less as surgical cutting and more as a broad sweep for savings. In addition, Microsoft’s 2026 annual report warns, in plain terms, that demand for all this AI capacity could be overestimated and could leave much of its infrastructure underused. Strip it back, and the push for voluntary exits is a statement of intent. Offering buyouts to more than a quarter of staff while pouring record sums into compute raises questions about whether Microsoft expects AI-driven productivity gains to change its long-term staffing needs. However, the company has said AI is not directly driving the buyout program, instead pointing to changing business priorities and workforce needs. The catch is timing. Microsoft is committing to the costs now and trusting the benefits to arrive later. The tests from here are familiar ones: whether Azure holds its current pace, whether Copilot usage hardens into durable revenue, and whether all that spending earns an acceptable return before investors run short of patience. They keep pointing to the engine behind the buyout logic: accelerating Azure growth, a massive contracted backlog, and full-stack AI monetization that’s turning Copilot and cloud usage into real revenue, all while Microsoft still throws off healthy free cash flow. That’s the bull case in a sentence: the AI spending is being matched by AI income. If that holds, a leaner, heavier-investing Microsoft looks like a company spending from strength. The risk never quite leaves; the returns still have to keep pace with the capital expenditure, but for now, the bullish case has plenty of support. title: Estée Lauder Expands Microsoft AI Partnership As It Targets Productivity, Personalized Experiences - TradingView
content: The Estée Lauder Companies (EL) announced a strategic partnership with Microsoft (MSFT) on Friday to strengthen its cloud and data infrastructure and support the responsible adoption of AI across its business. “Our partnership with Microsoft, in addition to the other strategic partners in our One Operating Ecosystem, is powering our teams with the capabilities to ultimately deliver more relevant, personalized experiences that meet consumers’ evolving needs,” said Brian Franz, chief technology and transformation officer at Estée Lauder. EL shares traded 2.5% lower, and MSFT shares traded 1.5% lower at the time of writing. Microsoft Copilot Reaches More Than 14,000 Employees Estée Lauder has expanded Microsoft Copilot across its global office-based workforce, reaching more than 14,000 employees. The partnership focuses on three strategic priorities: New Capabilities & Growth, Decision Intelligence, and Productivity & Automation. The company is also experimenting with productivity agents and embedding AI into role-specific workflows while automating repetitive manual tasks. Estée Lauder said these tools are intended to help employees focus on strategy, innovation, and higher-value decision-making. Partnership Targets Data, Consumer Insights, Product Development The collaboration will advance Estée Lauder’s Unified Data Platform, which connects data across brands, regions, channels and functions. The company said the platform is designed to reduce duplication, enable reusable data products and improve access to data-driven insights. The company is also investing in a Unified Consumer Data Platform to deepen its understanding of consumer needs and preferences. Combined with connected product data, the platform is designed to support personalized experiences from product discovery to purchase and inform product innovation, drawing on the company’s 80 years of consumer understanding and beauty expertise. Separately, Estée Lauder is developing a connected, AI-powered workflow across product design, validation and manufacturing. The initiative aims to help teams make faster, more coordinated decisions and move products from idea to launch more efficiently. Franz said the partnership’s enhanced capabilities would help Estée Lauder “drive sustainable growth, improve productivity, and support margin expansion,” while creating capacity for reinvestment. Microsoft Executive Vice President and Chief Revenue Officer Deb Cupp said the collaboration would help turn insights into action at scale, from empowering employees to modernizing product development and delivering more meaningful consumer experiences. The partnership supports Estée Lauder’s Beauty Reimagined strategy and forms part of its One Operating Ecosystem. It also locks in 40-year money while lenders are eager to supply it. Lenders therefore see paying for Oracle’s expansion as much riskier than paying for Microsoft’s. Microsoft was a latecomer to the borrowing wave. Brett Kozlowski of GW&K called the timing “opportunistic”. Still, the fact that Microsoft borrowed at all shows that even the strongest balance sheet now wants outside money for this cycle. The falling stock reflects a fair worry about spending, since Microsoft expects second-quarter capex of over $50 billion. That risk grows. It grows further if AI demand slows while borrowed money funds buybacks, or if repeated bond sales put pressure on the AAA rating. The test is the fiscal second-quarter earnings report. Microsoft guided for Azure growth of 49 to 50% in constant currency. The case for the stock weakens. If Azure falls short of that range while capex tops $50 billion, a close below the October 29 low of $519.56 would signal market agreement. title: MSFT Stock Reverses to $530 as Investors Fear Lower Capex Might Signal the End of AI Bubble Despite Microsoft Beating Quarterly Earnings and Revenue Expectations - FXLeaders
content: Microsoft stock reversed sharply after initially jumping above $550 following strong quarterly results, as lower-than-expected capital expenditure intensified questions about infrastructure demand, future returns and whether excessive spending which has inflated the AI bubble will start to dry up. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) shares initially jumped above $550 after the company reported stronger-than-expected quarterly earnings and revenue, supported by accelerating cloud growth. However, the rally quickly reversed, sending the stock below $530 and toward $520 as investors reassessed the company’s infrastructure spending plans. The immediate concern was not a lack of demand but the scale and pace of Microsoft’s investment. Total capital expenditure and finance leases reached $45.2 billion, approximately 30% higher year over year but below analysts’ average estimate of $50.7 billion. The shortfall has raised questions about the timing of infrastructure expansion and the potential returns from the massive investments being made across the technology sector. With major companies committing billions of dollars to computing infrastructure, investors are increasingly concerned that spending expectations have become difficult to sustain. Microsoft reported net income of $36.6 billion, or $4.92 per diluted share, representing a 32% increase on a GAAP basis. Non-GAAP earnings reached $4.89 per share, excluding the impact of investments in OpenAI. Revenue increased to $90.6 billion from $77.6 billion a year earlier, meeting Bloomberg’s analyst consensus estimate. Earnings comfortably exceeded expectations of $4.27 per share. The results demonstrate that Microsoft’s underlying business continues to expand despite growing scrutiny of its investment strategy. However, the market reaction suggests that strong financial performance alone may no longer be sufficient to sustain the stock’s upward momentum. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, increasing 30% year over year, or 31% in constant currency. Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said results exceeded expectations across revenue, operating income and earnings per share. Chief Executive Officer Satya Nadella highlighted Microsoft’s efforts to improve computing capability, customer choice, security and cost efficiency. Nevertheless, investors want evidence that strong demand will translate into attractive returns on infrastructure spending. Cloud growth remains a major strength, but the cost of expanding capacity could limit the financial benefits if revenue fails to keep pace with investment. Microsoft’s spending figures have become central to the debate over the sustainability of the technology rally. The company is expanding its computing infrastructure to support cloud services and growing demand for advanced computing, while other major technology companies are pursuing similarly expensive investment programmes. Elon Musk recently warned on X that more than 200 new cloud providers could face what he described as “guppy-level death and consolidation.” He argued that companies without substantial standalone revenue beyond data centres could struggle to secure financing in debt markets. His comments reflect broader concerns about whether infrastructure providers can generate sufficient revenue to justify their spending. If demand expectations weaken or financing becomes more expensive, companies with large commitments and limited cash generation could face significant pressure. For Microsoft, the issue is particularly important because investors have already priced in substantial future growth. Any indication that infrastructure demand is weaker than expected, or that returns are taking longer to materialise, could trigger further valuation adjustments. Microsoft shares jumped above the critical $500 level as they rebounded strongly in the last 2 months, climb above $550 earlier this week but slipped below $530 again. The price slip tested the 20 daily SMA in gray in September which has been acting as support. The $550 area represents both psychological and technical resistance so for now MAFT buyers gave up at this zone, revering lower. Microsoft’s stock has undergone a notable repricing in recent months, signaling a broader reset in how investors are assessing mega-cap technology leaders. After peaking above $555 in October 2025, shares retreated sharply, and despite the revival in 2026, buyers haven’t been able to break above that level. Microsoft’s Devices and Consumer segment generated $15.5 billion in revenue, down 3% year over year. Search and advertising revenue, excluding traffic acquisition costs, increased 12%. However, Xbox content and services revenue declined 2%, or 1% in constant currency, while Windows OEM and Devices revenue fell 22%. The contrasting performance highlights Microsoft’s dependence on its cloud business to sustain overall growth while some consumer-facing operations remain under pressure. Microsoft is developing its Maia 300 processor to improve computing efficiency and reduce reliance on external chip suppliers. The processor reportedly targets 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems, while its 96-accelerator configuration is designed to deliver up to seven times the rack-scale throughput of Maia 200. Custom silicon could eventually help Microsoft reduce computing costs. However, development and deployment require substantial investment, meaning the financial benefits will depend on successful implementation and sufficient demand. Microsoft has also reportedly discussed leasing computing capacity from SpaceX, although the current status of those talks remains unclear. Microsoft faces additional pressure from the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority, which has proposed designating the company as having strategic market status in certain software markets. The designation could lead to greater scrutiny of licensing, pricing and product bundling. Competition from Google Workspace also presents challenges as businesses reassess Microsoft 365 costs and features. Meanwhile, restructuring in Microsoft’s gaming division, including planned job reductions, highlights efforts to improve efficiency across its operations. Microsoft’s earnings and cloud growth remain strong, but the reversal below $530 suggests investors are becoming more selective about expensive infrastructure investments. Buyers will need to demonstrate that the stock can regain momentum above $530 and challenge the $550 area again. Failure to recover could leave shares vulnerable to further selling toward $520 and potentially $500 if negative sentiment intensifies. The central question is whether Microsoft’s expanding infrastructure will generate sufficient revenue and cash flow to justify the investment. Until investors gain greater confidence in those returns, concerns about excessive spending and a potential AI bubble could continue to weigh on the stock.

title: Microsoft (MSFT Stock) Q1 FY2027 Earnings Show Azure Surging 48% as AI Raises Energy Concerns - CarbonCredits.com
content: Microsoft (MSFT stock) reported strong first-quarter results for fiscal 2027 as demand for artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing and enterprise software continued to grow. Revenue reached $92.3 billion for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, up 19% year over year. Microsoft Cloud revenue climbed 30% to $63.9 billion, highlighting the growing importance of AI infrastructure to its business. However, this expansion brings a major sustainability challenge. Microsoft’s 2026 Environmental Sustainability Report shows that its greenhouse gas emissions rose 25% in fiscal 2025 as the company expanded its data centers and changed how it procures renewable electricity. The results highlight a growing tension for the technology giant: scaling AI services while working toward its goal of becoming carbon negative by 2030. Microsoft’s first-quarter results show continued strength across its cloud and AI businesses. The company also reported commercial remaining performance obligations of $677 billion, up 73% year over year. This represents contracted revenue that Microsoft expects to recognize in the future, although the timing depends on customer demand and contract terms. Microsoft returned $10.2 billion to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases during the quarter. CEO Satya Nadella highlighted the company’s technology capabilities, while CFO Amy Hood pointed to strong cloud growth and results that exceeded expectations for revenue, operating income, and earnings per share. Microsoft’s Agents and Infra segment generated $76.8 billion in revenue, up 25% year over year. Azure revenue increased 48% to $33.2 billion, while Microsoft 365 cloud revenue rose 17% to $27.8 billion. Industry solutions revenue increased 9% to $5.3 billion. Search and advertising revenue grew 10% to $6.6 billion. Other businesses showed mixed results. Windows OEM and devices revenue declined 22% to $3.6 billion, while Xbox revenue fell 2% to $5.4 billion. The Devices and Consumer segment generated $15.5 billion, down 3% year over year. These results show how cloud computing and AI are becoming central to the company’s growth. Microsoft shares (MSFT stock) gained more than 3% in after-hours trading following its October 28 earnings announcement, as Azure growth of 48% and stronger-than-expected results eased concerns about returns on AI infrastructure spending. The latest sustainability report shows that the company’s total greenhouse gas emissions increased 25% year over year. It attributed the rise mainly to expanding data-center infrastructure and its decision to stop using non-additional, unbundled renewable energy certificates as it prioritizes investments that bring new carbon-free electricity to power grids. This distinction matters. Renewable energy certificates can help companies account for renewable electricity, but they do not always lead to new clean energy generation. Microsoft is shifting toward projects and contracts intended to add new electricity supply. The latest report highlights the difficulty of reducing emissions while building data centers at speed. Microsoft’s climate strategy must address both the electricity used to operate its infrastructure and the carbon embedded in the materials and equipment required to expand it. Microsoft continues to improve data-center efficiency as demand for AI computing rises. Microsoft is also developing cooling technologies that reduce water demand. In its Phoenix data centers, cooling improvements delivered a 23% year-over-year reduction in WUE in FY2025. The company is extending similar improvements to other facilities. On clean electricity, it achieved its milestone of matching 100% of its annual global electricity consumption with renewable energy in FY2025. In February 2026, it reported that it had contracted 40 gigawatts of new renewable energy across 26 countries, with 19 GW already online. Matching electricity consumption with renewable energy is an important milestone, but it does not mean every data center runs entirely on renewable power at every hour. Grid conditions, project availability and the timing of electricity generation still matter. Microsoft also reported progress on water and waste. In FY2025, it replenished more than 14.2 million cubic meters of water, exceeding the amount it withdrew. The company achieved a 92% reuse and recycling rate for decommissioned cloud hardware, surpassing its 90% target for the second consecutive year. Reusing equipment and components can reduce waste and limit demand for new materials. Microsoft continues to invest in carbon removal as part of its plan to become carbon negative by 2030. Its 2026 report highlights an agreement with Rubicon Carbon to purchase up to 18 million metric tons of afforestation, reforestation and revegetation credits. These projects can help remove carbon from the atmosphere, but carbon removal alone cannot solve the emissions challenge. Microsoft must also reduce emissions from its operations, electricity purchases and supply chain. Microsoft’s latest earnings show that AI and cloud computing remain powerful growth drivers. Its sustainability report, however, shows that rising infrastructure demand continues to put pressure on its climate targets. For investors, the key question is whether Microsoft can improve efficiency, add new carbon-free electricity and cut supply-chain emissions fast enough to support its 2030 commitments. The company has made progress on renewable electricity, water replenishment and hardware reuse. Yet the 25% annual increase in emissions shows that its sustainability strategy faces a difficult test as AI infrastructure expands. title: The Memory Crunch Is Crushing Microsoft Windows PC Sales - 24/7 Wall St.
content: A global memory shortage is doing something no software competitor has managed: shrinking Microsoft's Windows business faster with each passing quarter, and the damage is spreading beyond PC makers into the data centers powering Microsoft's own AI ambitions. Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction) said on October 28, 2026, that its Windows business will shrink faster in the December quarter than in the September quarter it had just reported. The stock closed at $531.01 before the results. It then rose 2.90% to $546.39 in after-hours trading as of about 7:59 p.m. ET, because cloud strength offset the Windows warning. In this case, Windows sales means Windows OEM revenue, which is the license fees Microsoft collects from PC makers such as HP (NYSE:HPQ) and Dell Technologies (NYSE:DELL). That revenue moves with PC unit sales. The memory shortage that is pressuring those PC makers also raises what Microsoft pays to build data centers. 2026's Biggest AI Trends: The Memory Explosion | MU Stock, SNDK Stock, SK Hynix, CAMT Stock Devices and Consumer revenue was $15.5 billion, and Windows OEM and devices revenue fell 22%. That roughly matched the low-20s decline CFO Amy Hood guided for on July 29, 2026. The Windows OEM line by itself missed. Amy Hood said it fell 27%, or 28% in constant currency (excluding exchange-rate moves), the same rate Counterpoint Research expects PC shipments to fall in the December quarter. She said it was “below expectations” and pointed to “the Windows 10 end of support demand in the prior year, inventory drawdowns by OEM and channel partners and weaker PC market demand.” The first cause is a tough comparison, since a year earlier buyers rushed to upgrade as Windows 10 support ended. For the December quarter, Amy Hood said “Windows OEM and devices revenue should decline in the mid-30s” and guided Devices and Consumer revenue to $15.9 billion to $16.4 billion. She added, “We expect these trends to continue through the rest of the fiscal year.” The link to memory comes from Hood’s earlier comments. In January 2026, she highlighted “the potential impact on the PC market from increased memory pricing,” and on July 29, she said partners were building inventory “given increasing component prices.” PC makers stocked up ahead of price hikes and are now selling down that inventory. That helps explain why Amy Hood’s guided decline deepened from the low 20s to the mid-30s. Ben Yeh, a principal analyst at Omdia, said memory’s share of PC costs has risen from roughly 15% to nearly 40%. That cost squeeze cut September-quarter PC shipments 21% to 57 million, Counterpoint Research counted, with HP falling 31% and Dell 25%; it expects another 27% drop in the December quarter. Its senior analyst, Minsoo Kang, said: “rising memory and component costs push system prices higher and force consumers to delay replacement purchases.” PC makers have been slipping, with HP down 3.37% to $32.45 in the October 28 regular session, and Dell slipped 1.63% to $493.79. Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) rose 1.91% to $95.53, then dropped 2.55% to $93.09 after hours as of about 7:59 p.m. ET. Intel is expected to report on October 29, and HP and Dell are expected to report around November 24, although none of the three has confirmed its date. Amy Hood said about three-quarters of September-quarter capital spending went to short-lived assets, “primarily CPUs and GPUs, including higher memory and storage costs.” The same shortage that is cutting into Windows licensing also raises Microsoft’s data-center costs. Microsoft’s results still held up because Devices and Consumer is the smaller of its two segments. That data-center spending is going toward meeting AI demand from paying customers, and the suppliers wiring up those facilities, from power to cooling to networking, are the quieter beneficiaries of the same expansion (we covered seven of them in a free report on the AI infrastructure trade). A deeper Windows decline reduces a high-margin license stream, but it leaves the cloud business that drives Microsoft’s growth intact. A bottom in Windows would show up as partner inventories return to normal, memory prices ease, and the Windows 10 comparison drops out of the numbers. If the December-quarter earnings report shows Windows OEM and devices revenue falling further than Amy Hood’s mid-30s guide, the bullish case for Microsoft weakens. title: New Microsoft Price Target as $33 Billion Cloud Update Turns Heads - RealMoney Pro
content: Waiting for answers on 2027 free cash flow and capex questions could keep the shares capped near term. Microsoft (MSFT) delivered the kind of quarter investors have been waiting for from the AI buildout: accelerating cloud growth, guidance ahead of expectations and better than expected free cash flow that more than doubled what Wall Street had modeled. Coming into the company’s earnings call, we shared that we knew we had some catch up work to do with our MSFT price target. That combined with what we saw and heard on Wednesday night is leading us to boost that target to $600 from $500. Others across Wall Street are taking their MSFT targets higher, in some cases meaningfully higher. Wells Fargo reset its target at $750, and Citi is now at $680, while Morgan Stanley landed at $650. The key behind our price target and most likely those other ones is that Azure continues to deliver meaningful upside relative to market expectations despite capacity constraints. Azure revenue grew 48% to $33.2 billion versus the 44% Wall Street expected, and management guided for growth to pick up to 49% to 50% in the December quarter even with some third-party capacity slipping into 2027, because demand continues to exceed supply. Microsoft’s commercial backlog jumped 73% to $677 billion, equal to roughly 10.6 quarters of the $63.9 billion in Microsoft Cloud revenue it booked in the September quarter. Similar to what we saw with Q3 2026 results for Google’s (GOOGL) cloud segment, the operating income at Microsoft’s operating income for Agents and Infra rose at a brisker pace compared to its revenue. But the big difference between the two is the $18.6 billion in free cash flow Microsoft delivered versus the roughly $8.5 billion Wall Street modeled, while still returning $10.2 billion to shareholders. That said, like Meta (META), Google, and most likely as we’ll hear on Thursday from Amazon (AMZN), Microsoft expects to step up its capex spend in calendar 2027. This more than likely means Wall Street will need to revisit its free cash flow expectations for Microsoft when the company reports its current quarter in early January and lays out its calendar 2027 capex plans. Until we have greater clarity on that, and whether that free cash flow figure is a positive one or not and how its stacks up against Wall Street expectations, we are keeping our Two rating in play. Current consensus expectations have Microsoft delivering free cash flow near $30 billion in the current fiscal year that ends June 2027 and $35.6 billion for the one ending June 2028. Even though we can see upside to $600 for MSFT shares, waiting the answer to that question could keep MSFT shares range bound. Should Microsoft tap its investments in OpenAI and Databricks following IPOs for those companies, that would lead us, and most likely others, to revisit capex spend and potential cash flow dynamics. It would also have a role to play in revisiting our new MSFT target price. Before we move on to discuss Microsoft’s quarter, we’ll reiterate one of the comments we made regarding Google and eventual cash flow. When Microsoft’s AI buildout begins to temper and capex starts to decline, it stands to reason that Azure margins will lift and the company’s free cash flow reaccelerates. That’s the medium- to longer-term opportunity in the shares. For its fiscal first quarter of 2027, Microsoft’s revenue climbed 19% to $92.3 billion, ahead of the 17% growth and $90.6 billion analysts expected, and adjusted EPS of $4.89 topped the $4.71 consensus. What stands out to us is the operating leverage. Operating income rose 21% while operating expenses grew just 6%, and operating margin edged up to 50%. CFO Amy Hood credited efficiency gains across the GPU and CPU fleet that let Microsoft sell more capacity without adding cost, and that’s where internal AI use shows up in the numbers: throughput for Copilot workloads rose more than 50% from the June quarter, and in-house AI models are taking on more work at lower cost. Under the new segment structure, Agents and Infra revenue grew 25% to $76.8 billion, Microsoft Cloud revenue accelerated to 30% growth and Foundry revenue more than tripled. M365 commercial cloud grew 18% in constant currency on an adjusted basis, helped by GitHub Copilot, and management expects about 19% growth in the December quarter with acceleration through the fiscal year. The soft spot remains Devices and Consumer, where revenue fell 3% to $15.5 billion and Windows OEM and devices revenue is expected to fall in the mid-30% range in the December quarter on elevated PC inventory and a tough Windows 10 comparison. That Device and Consumer outlook should not be a surprise given the Q3 2026 drop in PC industry shipments. On the customer AI side, Microsoft is seeing adoption broaden. Copilot daily users rose nearly 50% from the June quarter and more than five-times year over year, the number of customers with more than 50,000 Copilot seats rose more than eight times, and the number of customers consuming Copilot credits through usage-based billing grew more than 75%. That shift from per-seat subscriptions to consumption expands Microsoft’s addressable market, though Hood cautioned it will move more slowly outside of coding. Those data points and others support the view that AI adoption is rising and usage expanding, and that reinforces our position on several holdings in the Portfolio that stand to benefit from the AI infrastructure build out as does the collective step up in AI and data center capex. For the December quarter, Microsoft guided revenue to $96.0 billion to $97.1 billion, above the $95.6 billion consensus, with operating margin down slightly year over year as Azure becomes a bigger part of the mix and costs from its latest employee buyout offer flow through. Capital spending for the quarter came in at $45.2 billion, below Microsoft’s own $50 billion forecast, largely because third-party capacity deliveries slipped, not because Microsoft pulled back. Still, that likely means Microsoft would have still delivered positive free cash flow for the quarter, more likely in-line with what Wall Street had forecasted. The larger question is It expects capex to top $50 billion in the December quarter, total about $170 billion for calendar 2026 and accelerate again in the first half of 2027 as those deliveries arrive and memory and storage costs climb. That along with Meta’s (META) step up in capex bodes well for Arista Networks (ANET) but as we’ve discussed capacity constraints could make for fits and starts for Arista’s deliverables. Microsoft added 24 new data centers across five continents in the quarter, installed its first Nvidia (NVDA) Vera Rubin GPUs and cut the time it takes to bring new GB300 capacity online by about 20%. Operating cash flow rose 29% to $58 billion, and capex consumed about 68% of it, compared with roughly 122% at Alphabet, which is why Microsoft generated $18.6 billion in free cash flow while Alphabet burned $9.1 billion. Granted, some of Microsoft’s upside is capex timing, and let’s remember it also leans on finance leases, $7.4 billion in the quarter, that don’t run through that cash figure. Even so, management expects to remain free cash flow positive in fiscal 2027 and will tap leasing or debt markets only “when we believe it is attractive to do so.” As we called out above, come January we’ll have a better indication for that free cash flow figure and how it stacks up against Wall Street’s models. At the time of publication, TheStreet Pro was long AMZN, ANET, GOOGL, META, MSFT and NVDA. title: Satya Nadella Says Renting AI Capacity to a Few Big Customers Is “Not a Business” - 24/7 Wall St.
content: Satya Nadella drew a sharp line between the AI customers Microsoft wants and the ones it will tolerate, and the distinction reveals something uncomfortable about how the biggest names in cloud infrastructure actually make their money. On the September-quarter earnings call of Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction), held October 28, 2026, Satya Nadella compared the enterprise customers he wants with “like 4 customers who buy a lot of capacity from you and you can show a few quarters of growth.” He added, “And that’s not a business as far as I’m concerned.” The remark came from results in which Microsoft reported revenue of $92.3 billion, up 19%, with Azure revenue up 48%. Shares closed at $531.01 before the release, down 0.06%, leaving the company worth $3.94 trillion. After the call, they traded at $546.39 at about 7:59 p.m. ET, up 2.90%. Microsoft (MSFT) The Least Magnificent of the Mag 7 - Time To Sell? A Bernstein Research analyst asked how much of Azure’s AI demand comes from enterprises. Satya Nadella said Rolls-Royce runs jet-engine maintenance across 30,000 parts on Foundry, Microsoft’s platform for building AI agents, and that Austrian bank RBI showed him 20-plus business processes end to end. These are recurring workflows that use compute every day, so they last longer than a one-time capacity purchase. Nadella did not name any company. He said Microsoft is “open for business” with large buyers because “as long as the pricing is right, we may sell them some.” Nadella told Morgan Stanley’s Adam Wood that “we have one pool and we want to get the pool to be as efficient and fungible.” Fungible capacity is hardware that can shift among many customers and workloads, which lowers the risk that one departing buyer leaves expensive chips idle. Amy Hood said capex of $45.2 billion came in below her July 29 guide of over $50 billion “as some third-party capacity deliveries we expected in Q1 were delayed.” She added that “Customer demand continues to exceed available supply.” For the December quarter, Amy Hood guided Azure growth of 49% to 50% in constant currency and capex of over $50 billion, with calendar-year spending of approximately $170 billion. A company that is short on supply can afford to be choosy on price, so the stance costs Microsoft little. Commercial remaining performance obligation, which is contracted revenue not yet recognized, rose 73% to $677 billion, while commercial bookings fell 12%. Hood tied the decline to “large Azure commitments in the prior year,” partly offset by “a large Azure commitment this quarter.” Microsoft also recorded $10.0 billion of revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI out of $92.279 billion, or about 10.8%. It also buys third-party capacity, so it sits on both sides of the model Nadella questioned. For comparison, CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) closed at $63.93 on October 28. For the June 2026 quarter, it reported three unnamed customers at 36%, 26% and 10% of revenue. Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) closed at $144.54 with $638 billion of remaining performance obligations. S&P Global Ratings (SGR) estimates OpenAI accounts for roughly half of that total. Microsoft’s results support its growth case. Demand is running ahead of supply, so capacity is what limits revenue, and the growing backlog shows customers are signing commitments years in advance. The risks are heavy capex, delayed third-party deliveries, and the share of revenue that comes from OpenAI. Spreading AI across many enterprise workflows is how Microsoft reduces that concentration over time, and this quarter showed that spread growing. All of that capex has to be powered and cooled by somebody, which is why the suppliers behind the data centers keep showing up alongside the hyperscalers themselves. We pulled together seven of them in a free report on the AI infrastructure buildout. Microsoft has not confirmed the date of its next report. If Azure growth falls short of Amy Hood’s 49% to 50% guidance, or OpenAI’s share of revenue rises above about 10.8%, the case for breadth gets weaker. title: OpenAI Now Makes Up 11% of Microsoft’s Revenue - 24/7 Wall St.
content: Microsoft's latest quarterly filing reveals it partly owns one of its biggest customers, and the money flowing between them is growing faster than most investors realize. Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction) filed its quarterly report for the three months ended September 30 with the SEC on October 28, 2026. It shows $10.0 billion of revenue from OpenAI, out of total revenue of $92.279 billion at Microsoft. That is about 10.8%, which means Microsoft partly owns one of its largest customers. The stock closed at $531.01, down 0.06%. After hours, it rose 2.90% to $546.39 as of about 7:59 p.m. ET. OpenAI revenue helps justify Microsoft’s data center expansion, but it also links more of the payback to one private customer that needs a lot of cash. The filing calls the figure “revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, inclusive of revenue-sharing payments,” so it covers more than Azure cloud purchases. Microsoft reports it because OpenAI is an equity-method investee, meaning Microsoft owns enough of it to count its share of OpenAI’s results, and that makes OpenAI a related party. Goldman Sachs analyst Gabriela Borges rounded the share to 11% on the earnings call, telling CEO Satya Nadella, “you have OpenAI at 11% of revenue in the quarter.” Microsoft itself did not give that number. In fiscal 2026, OpenAI was about 7.3% of revenue: $24.1 billion out of $331.839 billion. The September quarter alone produced roughly 41% of that full-year total. OpenAI owed Microsoft $7.2 billion at September 30, up from $6.0 billion at June 30. That is a 20% rise in three months. Receivables are bills sent but not yet paid, so this rise means Microsoft is giving more trade credit to a company it partly owns. Microsoft holds “an approximate 24% interest on an as-converted basis,” down from about 25% at June 30. It has paid $12.0 billion of its $13.0 billion commitment. Other income showed net profits of $272 million on OpenAI investments, compared with net losses of $4.1 billion a year earlier. As a result, GAAP EPS of $4.92 came close to non-GAAP EPS of $4.89, which excludes the OpenAI impact. Revenue grew 19% to $92.3 billion from $77.673 billion. Net income rose 32% to $36.6 billion, and Azure grew 48%. Growth this broad would likely still look strong without OpenAI. A rising share also gives OpenAI more leverage on price, because Microsoft needs its workloads to fill the new capacity it is building, and that capacity story goes well beyond the chipmakers (we covered seven suppliers of power, cooling, and networking behind the data-center boom here). Nadella said coding-agent users want “Anthropic and OpenAI, by the way, to compete for your workload, not like once a quarter, but for every task.” Microsoft says its own MAI models target “capabilities comparable to leading models within 3 to 6 months of their release at a fraction of the training cost.” CFO Amy Hood said capital spending (capex) of $45.2 billion came in lower “as some third-party capacity deliveries we expected in Q1 were delayed.” Hood expects December-quarter capex of over $50 billion. Hood put calendar 2026 spending at approximately $170 billion, slightly below her July 29 guidance of about $175 billion. Free cash flow was $18.6 billion, and Hood expects it to stay positive through fiscal 2027. Microsoft’s fundamentals look solid. Net income is growing faster than revenue while capex continues to rise, and free cash flow remains positive. The OpenAI concentration and the rising receivables are real risks. But Microsoft discloses them, and its MAI models give it a fallback if OpenAI gains more pricing power. Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG, NASDAQ:GOOGL) fell 9.97% after hours to $292.50 from a $324.89 close. At that close, it was worth $3.97 trillion, compared with Microsoft at $3.94 trillion. At after-hours prices as of about 7:59 p.m. ET on October 28, Microsoft’s implied value of about $4.05 trillion was above Alphabet’s about $3.57 trillion. That is only an estimate until the October 29 close confirms it. Microsoft’s next quarterly report is expected in late January 2027, although the company has not confirmed the date. If it shows OpenAI’s share still rising, receivables above $7.2 billion, and the stake below the approximate 24% level, concern about Microsoft’s dependence on OpenAI grows. title: Alphabet tanks nearly 13% for worst day ever, losing $500 billion in value - CNBC
content:
Alphabet shares plunged the most since Google went public in 2004, dropping 13% on Thursday, wiping out roughly $500 billion in market cap. In its earnings announcement late Wednesday, Alphabet reported negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion for the third quarter, compared to the $2.7 billion analysts expected. The Google parent maintained its full year capital expenditure guidance of between $195 billion and $205 billion. Microsoft, meanwhile, traded largely flat as investors focused on the tech giants’ latest spending and free cash flow numbers in the third-quarter earnings report. Microsoft reported $45.2 billion in capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, which was 30% higher than a year ago, but below analyst projections of $50.67 billion. Free cash flow fell 27% to $18.63 billion but remained positive. The earnings reports come as investors scrutinize AI spending plans of tech companies and are focusing on the returns on those investments. “Microsoft is building out its architecture in a measured way and as such contains fewer surprises,” Ben Barringer, global head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, said on Thursday. “Alphabet, by contrast, saw its share price hit after hours as a result of a fairly messy set of results and a poorly handled earnings call” . Alphabet’s biggest source of revenue, search advertising, grew 12% in the September quarter to $63.35 billion, but missed analyst expectations, adding further pressure to the company’s shares. Philipp Schindler, Alphabet’s chief business officer, said the impact on the search business was partly because of lower monetization within the company’s AI Mode. He added that Alphabet is now “scaling” ads within its AI Overviews and AI Mode products, including in international markets. Google’s search business has faced headwinds from the rise of other AI chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude. People may be carrying out more search queries outside Google. Gemini, Google’s own AI chatbot, has failed to keep pace. “The problem for Google is it faces an innovator’s dilemma and doesn’t know whether to protect its core business or look to join the disruption. As such, Google has lost its edge with Gemini and is behind peers on agentic AI,” Barringer said. Google’s dominant market share in the search business, however, could ultimately give it a leg up over its peers, Rosenblatt Securities analyst Scott Devitt said. “I don’t think it’s a sea change,” Devitt told CNBC’s “Squawk on the Street” on Thursday. “If it’s a problem for Alphabet, it’s a problem for any consumer-facing AI agent or LLM as well. And so, it’s a problem that I think is ultimately going to be resolved. And when it does, Alphabet, with its 4 billion search customers that become AI customers, is in an enviable position.” - CNBC’s Robert Hum, Samantha Subin, Jordan Novet and Caleigh Keating contributed reporting. Microsoft Cloud revenue surpassed $63 billion with growth accelerating to 30% year over year, driven by strong demand across Azure and M365 commercial cloud. Copilot momentum is strong: daily users up nearly 50% quarter over quarter and over 5x year over year, with customer satisfaction at an all-time high and large seat purchases growing over 8x year over year. Foundry revenue more than tripled year over year, with over 120,000 customers, and Azure revenue grew 48% (ahead of expectations) despite capacity delays. Operating income increased 21% and operating margins remained strong at 50%, showcasing operational efficiency and revenue growth. Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT) continues to innovate with first-party models (e.g., MAI Cyber, MAI Transcribe) delivering cost and performance benefits, and infrastructure expansion added 24 new data centers across five continents. Commercial bookings decreased 12% and 11% in constant currency, driven by the impact from large Azure commitments in the prior year, indicating potential volatility in bookings. Windows OEM revenue decreased 27% and is expected to decline in the mid-30s next quarter due to elevated inventory levels, weaker PC market demand, and prior-year comparables. Devices and Consumer revenue declined 3%, with Xbox revenue down 2% and hardware revenue expected to decline further, reflecting challenges in the consumer segment. Capital expenditures were $45.2 billion, with some third-party capacity deliveries delayed, and CapEx is expected to exceed $50 billion next quarter, impacting free cash flow which was $18.6 billion. Gross margin percentage declined year over year to 66% for Microsoft Cloud due to sales mix shift to Azure, and operating margins are expected to be down slightly next quarter. Q: Karl Keirstead (UBS) asked Amy Hood to unpack the key drivers behind the surprisingly strong Azure growth guidance of 49% to 50% in constant currency for Q2. A: CFO Amy Hood explained that Q1 benefited from significant platform-layer efficiency gains across GPUs, CPUs, and the app stack, which allowed Microsoft to allocate more capacity to Foundry. She noted that higher-than-expected token pricing for high-quality models also contributed. For Q2, the guidance relies on continuing these efficiency gains to offset some third-party supply delays that shifted to the second half of the fiscal year, while acknowledging potential variability from token pricing. Q: Adam Wood (Morgan Stanley) asked whether improving utilization and unit costs within Azure or the ability to monetize more layers (Fabric, Foundry, Copilot) will be the more important driver of returns on AI capacity investments. A: CEO Satya Nadella stated it is "all of the above," emphasizing that Microsoft manages one fungible pool of infrastructure. He explained that margin leverage will come from every layerfrom the Copilot stateful database (WorkIQ) to Foundry for multi-agent systems, Azure databases like PostgreSQL, and security via Agent 365 and Perceptioncompounding when worked across the entire stack. Q: Mark Moerdler (Bernstein) asked for color on the mix of enterprise versus digitally native customers driving AI strength in Azure, and what is driving the growth of the Azure AI platform. A: CEO Satya Nadella highlighted a shift toward broad enterprise adoption, citing examples like Unilever's automated order-taking and Rolls-Royce's supply chain management built on Foundry. He noted that enterprises are increasingly focused on building systems they can own, manage costs for, and secure, rather than chasing "shiny objects." He characterized this enterprise breadth motion as a decade-long opportunity rather than a short-term trend driven by a few large customers. Q: Gabriela Borges (Goldman Sachs) asked how token mix and value will evolve between frontier models (like OpenAI) and Microsoft's first-party MAI models, given the goal of making MAI comparable to leading models within three to six months. A: CEO Satya Nadella described a dynamic toolbox for customers: they may start with a new frontier model, then use multiple frontier models via routers like Copilot Fusion for cost/performance optimization, and ultimately train their own models (open weights or MAI) using their own traces. He emphasized that Microsoft wants to provide a model system that delivers continuous value, allowing customers to switch between options based on pricing and needs rather than being locked into one approach. Q: Brent Thill (Jefferies) asked how Microsoft can sustain ~50% top-line growth alongside ~50% operating margins, and what operational improvements support this. A: CFO Amy Hood emphasized that revenue growth is the primary solution, starting at the top of the P&L. She noted that efficiency improvements are not just about cost reduction but about operational excellencedelivering the highest-quality unit at the lowest cost, which improves stability, security, and reliability. She also highlighted a focus on directing operating expenses toward building new products and ensuring security and quality. Q: Brad Reback (Stifel) asked whether the shift to consumption-based models for core M365 tools will unlock revenue quickly or require significant sales effort, similar to GitHub's transition. A: CEO Satya Nadella said the coding side (GitHub) will move faster because customers are already used to pay-as-you-go models, and tools like Copilot Fusion make credit usage more efficient. For M365 Copilot, Microsoft is driving value into the subscription (funded by IT for broad deployment) while offering consumption meters for additional needs. CFO Amy Hood added that the investment in the "frontier company" (FDE organization) and changes in sales motions are meant to help customers utilize both licenses and consumption meters optimally, though this transition will be slower outside of coding. Q: Tal Liani (Bank of America) asked about Microsoft's capital strategy, specifically how it intends to raise capital if needed, and whether Copilot numbers were disclosed this quarter. A: CFO Amy Hood stated Microsoft has significant flexibility, including leasing (already in use), debt markets (given strong ratings, though not yet tapped), and other options. She expressed confidence in being free cash flow positive and in the returns on CapEx, allowing the company to tap financing markets when attractive. She also confirmed that Microsoft did not disclose an updated Copilot number this quarter, focusing instead on momentum in revenue and usage. Q: Adam Wood (Morgan Stanley) asked about the drivers of returns on AI capacity, specifically utilization/unit costs versus monetizing more layers. A: CEO Satya Nadella reiterated that Microsoft views its infrastructure as a single efficient pool, with returns coming from every layerCopilot, WorkIQ, Foundry, Azure databases, and securitycompounding across the stack. CFO Amy Hood added that engineering efficiency gains at the platform layer in Q1 allowed more capacity allocation to Foundry, which is critical for customers building on the new stack. Q: Karl Keirstead (UBS) asked about the variables behind the Q2 Azure guidance of 49% to 50% constant currency growth. A: CFO Amy Hood explained that Q1 saw strong efficiency gains across the platform, enabling more Foundry allocation, and benefited from higher token pricing. For Q2, the guidance assumes continued efficiency gains to offset third-party supply delays shifted to H2, while acknowledging potential variability from token pricing and the timing of capacity additions. Q: Mark Moerdler (Bernstein) asked about the enterprise versus digitally native mix in Azure AI growth. A: CEO Satya Nadella emphasized that enterprise breadth is starting to materialize, with customers like Unilever and Rolls-Royce building complex agentic systems on Foundry. He noted that enterprises are focused on owning their systems, managing costs, and ensuring security, and that this breadth motion is a long-term opportunity rather than a short-term spike from a few large customers. MSFT shares were up 2.8% in pre-market trading. The stock has been on a positive streak lately and is on track for a fourth consecutive-month gain. The firm highlighted Microsoft’s ability to deliver strong Azure growth despite delays in expanding its data center capacity. While capital expenditures were lower than expected due to delays in capacity additions, Microsoft drove efficiencies across Azure that enabled the Q1 earnings beat and the guidance for 49-50% growth next quarter. Bernstein expects these efficiencies to benefit margins and performance in future years. Microsoft reported Q1 revenue of $92.28 billion, up 19% and ahead of Wall Street estimates of $90.61 billion. Adjusted earnings rose to $4.89 per share, beating expectations of $4.72, according to Fiscal.ai. Azure revenue jumped 48%, Microsoft Cloud revenue climbed 30% to $63.9 billion, while adjusted Microsoft 365 Commercial Cloud revenue rose 18%. However, the Devices and Consumer business remained weak, with revenue declining 3%. The company expects Q2 revenue to come in between $96 and $97.1 billion. Microsoft reported $45.2 billion in capex and finance leases in Q1, and while up about 30% from a year earlier, it came in below the company’s own target of around $50 billion. Piper Sandler raised its target to $650 from $610 and maintained an ‘Overweight’ rating. The firm highlighted Microsoft’s ability to improve infrastructure efficiency and noted that daily Copilot users increased nearly 50% quarter-over-quarter.
