Amazon (AMZN) could soon acquire Viasat (VSAT), while AST SpaceMobile (ASTS) has tried to assemble a rival bid, satellite consultant Tim Farrar said, outlining a potential takeover battle as Amazon and SpaceX compete for satellite dominance. Farrar pointed to growing expectations of an Amazon-Viasat deal in his recent note, “Prepare for the Musk vs Bezos cage fight,” following the Satellite Innovation conference in California. “But that’s mainly a telecom industry issue, and what was animating numerous people I spoke to yesterday, is the expectation that Amazon will soon announce the acquisition of Viasat, mainly for their international spectrum holdings, but also to combine Viasat’s Ka-band GEO business with Amazon Leo, and strengthen Amazon’s position in the government and aviation market (and incidentally remove Telesat’s biggest commercial customer for Lightspeed),” he said. In his view, pairing Viasat’s spectrum and geostationary satellites with Amazon’s low Earth orbit network could boost its government and aviation business, while sharpening its challenge to SpaceX. AST SpaceMobile’s rival effort would face funding and management hurdles, according to Farrar. “I’m also told AST has attempted to put together a rival bid, but that would require significant support from the telcos, and would be vehemently opposed by Viasat management,” he said. “In contrast, selling Viasat to Amazon could be seen as a graceful exit, before Viasat’s current GEO business is overwhelmed by LEO competition.” However, Farrar did not disclose a potential deal value or name the telecom companies that might back AST. He also predicted an Amazon takeover would end Equatys, Viasat’s venture with Space42, as a satellite project. But Amazon would still need to work with Space42 to coordinate L-band spectrum access in Europe, the Middle East and Africa. The speculation comes shortly after the FCC approved Amazon’s $11.5 billion Globalstar acquisition, advancing its push into direct-to-device satellite connectivity. The deal is expected to close in 2027. It would give Amazon 25 megahertz of internationally harmonized mobile-satellite spectrum and infrastructure to connect phones and other devices directly to satellites. The FCC said the deal could expand coverage, strengthen emergency communications, and put the spectrum to greater use, with no likely material public-interest harms. Amazon also has a pending application for up to 5,105 D2D satellites and has agreed to continue supporting Apple’s satellite services. Farrar said telecom operators are increasingly seeing Amazon as a counterweight to SpaceX. “In the D2D market, Amazon is seen as the most realistic potential savior by the telcos, as belief that AST will ever deliver a useful service ebbs away,” he said. Still, a telecom joint venture appeared poised to sign memorandums of understanding with both companies, he added. Amazon’s rollout speed and potential U.S. capacity also is uncertain. Farrar flagged risks in AST’s Ligado spectrum arrangement. “And AST’s relationship with Ligado remains tense: Ligado does not benefit at all from the high valuations now being put on MSS spectrum, because AST pays Ligado just enough to cover the ongoing lease payments to Viasat,” he said. He suggested that Ligado could surrender spectrum rights in a U.S. government settlement, potentially leaving AST exposed. Farrar linked the “missing pieces” Musk mentioned during SpaceX’s results call last week to a possible stock-based acquisition of EchoStar’s remaining business. In Farrar’s view, a deal could give SpaceX DISH Wireless network assets and additional AWS-3 and CBRS spectrum, while potentially replacing cash payments for previously agreed AWS-4 and Band 70 purchases. “And it would not be surprising if the deal was announced as soon as next week, given that mediation is scheduled through November 4, although Ergen is known for being a tough negotiator and might make it hard to reach an agreement on price,” Farrar said. title: What Microsoft (MSFT) Said on Its Q1 Earnings Call - TradingView
content: Microsoft MSFT reported a fast start to fiscal 2027, with first-quarter revenue of $92.3 billion, up 19% from a year earlier, as demand for cloud infrastructure and artificial intelligence services lifted results above the company’s expectations. Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said operating income increased 21%, while earnings per share rose 18% to $4.89. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, growing 30%, with growth accelerating from the prior quarter. The company’s operating margin increased slightly to 50% despite continued spending on AI infrastructure, research and development, and talent. “Our results exceeded expectations across revenue, operating income, and earnings per share, driven by strong demand across the Microsoft Cloud,” Hood said. Azure revenue rose 48% year over year, exceeding Microsoft’s expectations despite delays in some third-party capacity deliveries. Hood attributed the performance to Foundry, Microsoft’s platform for building and deploying AI agents, as well as improved monetization of CPU capacity. Foundry revenue more than tripled from a year earlier, while the number of Foundry customers exceeded 120,000. Chief Executive Officer Satya Nadella said customers are increasingly using the platform to build agentic systems that connect models, data and business workflows. Revenue from open-source models on Foundry increased tenfold, while the number of customers using multiple models for agentic solutions grew fivefold. Nadella said Microsoft’s AI strategy centers on delivering a connected stack that spans infrastructure, data, agent-building tools, workplace software and security. He described the company’s Copilot offerings as “the new OS for work,” saying daily users increased nearly 50% sequentially and more than fivefold year over year. Microsoft also said the number of customers with more than 50,000 Copilot seats rose more than eightfold year over year. Volkswagen, for example, announced plans to deploy Copilot to more than 330,000 employees, according to Nadella. Usage-based demand is also growing. The number of Copilot customers actively consuming credits through usage-based billing increased more than 75% during the quarter. On GitHub, agent-generated pull requests increased sixfold in the past six months and now account for more than one-third of pull requests on the platform, Nadella said. Microsoft spent $45.2 billion on capital expenditures during the quarter, although Hood said some expected third-party capacity deliveries were delayed. Roughly three-quarters of the spending went toward short-lived assets, primarily CPUs and GPUs, including memory and storage. The company added 24 data centers across five continents during the quarter and said it reduced dock-to-live times for new GB300 systems in its largest regions by about 20% sequentially. Microsoft also increased throughput for Copilot workloads by more than 50% from the prior quarter. For the second quarter, Microsoft expects capital expenditures to exceed $50 billion. Calendar-year spending is expected to be about $170 billion, with spending accelerating in the second half as delayed third-party capacity arrives along with additional CPU and GPU deployments. Hood said customer demand for Azure continues to exceed available supply. She said engineering improvements across GPUs, CPUs, storage, memory and application layers allowed Microsoft to allocate more capacity to Foundry customers during the first quarter. Higher-than-expected token pricing for certain AI models also benefited revenue. Microsoft expects Azure revenue growth of 49% to 50% in constant currency in the second quarter. Hood cautioned that quarterly growth may vary based on infrastructure efficiency gains, new capacity additions, model mix and the timing of large commitments. Microsoft 365 Commercial Cloud revenue increased 18%, or 19% in constant currency after adjusting for a prior-year comparison. The company cited stronger GitHub Copilot adoption and usage, partly offset by weaker sales execution for Microsoft 365 E3 and standalone products. Paid Microsoft 365 commercial seats rose 5%, with expansion primarily in small and midsize businesses and frontline worker offerings. Hood said growth in the commercial cloud business was driven by both average revenue per user and seat growth, with premium products including Microsoft 365 Copilot, E5 and E7 contributing to pricing gains. Devices and Consumer revenue fell 3% to $15.5 billion. Windows OEM and Devices revenue declined 22%, while Windows OEM revenue fell 27%, reflecting the prior-year benefit from Windows 10 end-of-support demand, inventory drawdowns by OEMs and channel partners, and weaker PC-market demand. Xbox revenue declined 2%, as growth in first-party content was offset by lower third-party content and Game Pass revenue. Search and advertising revenue excluding traffic acquisition costs rose 12%, driven by higher volume and rates across LinkedIn, Edge and Bing. Microsoft forecast total second-quarter revenue of $96 billion to $97.1 billion, representing growth of 18% to 19%. It expects Agents and Infra revenue of $80.1 billion to $80.7 billion, up 24% to 25%. Microsoft expects second-quarter operating expenses to rise about 9%, as it continues investing in R&D, compute capacity and talent. Hood said the company expects operating margin to decline slightly from the prior year, while remaining free-cash-flow positive for fiscal 2027. Microsoft Corporation MSFT is a global technology company that develops software, cloud services, devices and digital platforms. Its products and services are used by consumers, businesses, governments and educational institutions worldwide. The company's principal offerings include the Windows operating system; Microsoft 365 productivity applications such as Word, Excel, Teams and Outlook; Azure cloud computing and infrastructure services; Dynamics business applications; and enterprise security solutions. Microsoft reported Q1 revenue of $92.3 billion, up 19%, with Microsoft Cloud reaching $63.0 billion, a 30% increase; Q2 guidance is set at $96.0 billion, and full-year capital expenditures are projected to be approximately $170.0 billion. Zhitong Finance APP reports that Microsoft (MSFT.US) announced its financial results for the first quarter of fiscal year 2027 on Wednesday. The data shows that the company's revenue for the quarter reached $92.279 billion, a year-on-year increase of 19%; GAAP net profit was $36.629 billion, up 32% from $27.747 billion in the same period last year; GAAP diluted earnings per share (EPS) were $4.92, higher than $3.72 in the same period last year, representing a year-on-year increase of 32%. Non-GAAP adjusted net profit reached $36.422 billion, a year-on-year increase of 18%; adjusted EPS was $4.89, higher than $4.13 in the same period last year, representing a year-on-year increase of 18%. Microsoft stated that non-GAAP performance figures exclude the impact of its investment in OpenAI. In terms of profitability, Microsoft's operating profit for the first fiscal quarter reached $45.915 billion, a year-on-year increase of 21%, or 22% on a constant currency basis; the operating margin was approximately 49.8%, higher than 48.9% in the same period last year. Gross profit for the quarter was $62.559 billion, a year-on-year increase of approximately 17%, with a gross margin of approximately 67.8%. Below is the full transcript of Microsoft's earnings conference call (translated with the assistance of AI tools): The fiscal year has started strong. Microsoft Cloud revenue surpassed $63 billion, with growth accelerating to 30% year-on-year. The company is focusing on three key areas: designing AI that empowers humanity, ensuring every organization maintains sovereignty over its own learning, and building trust through control measures that ensure the safety and security of agents. Next, I will discuss how the company is building a new technology stack around these goals, starting with Copilot. This quarter, the company released its largest Copilot update to date, integrating chat, collaboration, autopilot, and code into a unified experience. This is an integrated product experience covering both commercial and consumer sectors, with the full suite of Office built-in. The company views Copilot as the new operating system for work. Customers are increasingly leveraging Copilot to accomplish actual work tasks. Automated task execution has nearly doubled since July; daily active users increased by nearly 50% month-over-month and more than fivefold year-over-year; user satisfaction improved by nearly 20% month-over-month, reaching a new historical high; 90% of Copilot queries use the auto mode, which dynamically routes tasks to different models to optimize for quality, speed, and cost. These improvements are translating into larger-scale procurement. The number of customers with more than 50,000 Copilot seats increased by more than eightfold year-over-year, including Capgemini, HCL Tech, Hitachi Group, Truist Financial, and His Majesty's Revenue and Customs (UK). Just last week, Volkswagen announced plans to deploy Copilot to more than 330,000 employees, marking one of the largest deployments in Europe to date. The E7 suite (integrating Copilot E5, Entra, and Agent 365) is gaining strong momentum, with thousands of customers across various industries having purchased it so far, including Amadeus, BlackRock, Fiserv, and the New South Wales Ministry of Health. The company's business model is expanding from seat-based subscriptions to include consumption-based models, thereby expanding the total addressable market (TAM) and average revenue per user (ARPU). Subscriptions deliver increasingly powerful daily intelligence to each user, typically funded by IT departments, integrating and rolling out cutting-edge capabilities across the entire organization; whereas when agents undertake higher-value work, the consumption model unlocks demand funded by business units, with spending directly linked to the value delivered by these agents. The number of Copilot customers actively consuming credits through pay-as-you-go billing increased by more than 75% this quarter. In the field of software development, all major coding agents have been launched on GitHub. Over the past six months, pull requests (PRs) generated by agents have grown sixfold, with agents currently initiating more than one-third of PRs on the platform. The company is focusing on enhancing reliability to handle the scaling of agent activity on GitHub. At the GitHub Universe conference this morning, the company demonstrated how to scale computing power for the wave of agents and refactor the core Git architecture; it also announced the general availability of Copilot Fusion, bringing multi-model orchestration to software development, which can accelerate speeds by up to 40% and reduce costs by 77%. Since the implementation of pay-as-you-go billing, credit consumption for agent features on GitHub has more than doubled. The company is also helping developers secure their code, transforming AI-generated code into high-quality software. GitHub Advanced Security revenue increased by more than 50% year-over-year, with customers leveraging its AI capabilities to scan entire codebases and remediate vulnerabilities in real time. In the commercial sector, the company continues to advance its vision of "Copilot as the new operating system for work," integrating Dynamics 365 business logic and capabilities directly into Copilot to help every organization build its own "infinite SaaS factory." This quarter, the company launched 30 new Copilot skills within Dynamics 365, enabling customers to invoke CRM and ERP capabilities directly within their workflows. In the recruitment sector, over 10 million LinkedIn members use AI-driven job search daily, and 25,000 customers utilize the company’s agent-based recruiting solutions. Recruiters using the hiring assistant find candidates meeting interview-quality standards 33% faster, while reducing the number of resumes reviewed to identify qualified candidates by 83%. In healthcare, the company automated 30 million patient encounters this quarter, a 70% year-over-year increase, helping clinicians reduce administrative burdens and spend more time with patients. Ten healthcare providers, including Advocate Health, Mass General Brigham, Mercy, and Intermountain Health, have each recorded over one million encounters using the company’s solutions since the beginning of the calendar year. In scientific research, the company’s Frontline Deployment Engineers (FDE) collaborate with customers to accelerate scientific progress using Discovery. A notable example is Saint-Gobain, which leverages Discovery to accelerate the development of low-carbon building materials. Underpinning these first-party agent experiences is a unified platform, led by Foundry, which is increasingly becoming a significant growth driver. Foundry helps organizations build learning loops rooted in their business contexts and deploy agents securely at scale. The company currently has over 120,000 Foundry customers, with revenue growing more than threefold year-over-year. Foundry’s model selection and feature set, combined with its deep integration into the company’s technology stack, are creating differentiation. Azure OpenAI benefited directly last quarter from significant advancements in OpenAI models; coupled with Foundry’s built-in model selection capabilities, customers can build solutions optimized for quality, cost, and performance. Indeed, the number of customers building agent solutions using multiple models grew fivefold year-over-year, and revenue from open-source models on Foundry increased tenfold. The company’s first-party models continue to advance rapidly. The company aims to push the "cost-to-outcome frontier," delivering comparable performance at a fraction of the training cost within three to six months of leading model releases, thereby passing these cost benefits to customers. This is already evident in current products: MAI-Cyber now supports over 40% of scans in the MDASH code scanner, reducing the cost per scan by 18%; MAI-Transcribe is the world’s most accurate and affordable transcription model, supporting multilingual workflows in Dragon Copilot; MAI-Code-Flash reached 3 million users on GitHub alone last month, helping developers use AI credits more efficiently; and Microsoft-Decision-1, the company’s new model for structured decision-making, outperforms LLMs and other decision models in both latency and quality, gaining over 4,000 customers in its first month, including Atos Group, Equinor, and Raiffeisen Bank International (RBI). The company recently completed pre-training for MAI-Base-2, which demonstrated 4 to 12 times higher training compute efficiency than other open-weight models in testing; this foundation model will underpin subsequent MAI models for inference, code, and cybersecurity. Beyond models, the company is opening the framework supporting its own Copilot experiences to Foundry customers, offering a Microsoft-managed approach to build agents capable of reasoning, tool invocation, and completing complex, long-running tasks, while retaining customer choice of models. Another critical layer is data. The company now has 44,000 paying Fabric customers, a year-over-year increase of over 50%. The company is tightening the integration between Foundry and Fabric, enabling customers to build their own agents alongside their data. Currently, over 19,000 customers use both Foundry and Fabric, allowing enterprises to connect and operate agents based on real-time operational, analytical, and unstructured data. Customers are also rapidly deploying the company’s AI-optimized databases, including PostgreSQL, SQL DB Hyperscale, and Cosmos DB, to provide agents with fast and secure access to data and context. PostgreSQL growth accelerated for the fourth consecutive quarter, with the number of PostgreSQL customers using Foundry increasing by 90% year-over-year. The company also possesses one of the most important databases for any enterprise—the knowledge graph underlying Microsoft 365, encompassing people, their relationships, documents, emails, meetings, chats, projects, and other assets. Work IQ provides this context to every agent workload. Leveraging Microsoft IQ, the company integrates Work IQ, Fabric IQ, and Foundry IQ into a unified context for agent systems. Nearly 60,000 customers are accessing context via Microsoft IQ, representing a 25% quarter-over-quarter increase. As enterprises deploy more agents, scalable governance becomes essential. Through Agent 365, the company provides an AI observability platform that enables customers to manage, secure, and optimize agent performance and costs. The registry currently contains over 50 million agents, a more than 30% increase quarter-over-quarter. Finally, as agents gain broader access to enterprise data and systems, security becomes increasingly critical. The company’s approach separates "intelligence" from "permissions," enforcing identity, access rights, monitoring, and containment outside the model. Last week, the company expanded new capabilities in Perception to help customers protect and contain insider threats from agents, including agent discovery in on-premises and cloud environments, dynamic least-privilege access for each task, and continuous risk assessment. The company also launched the Guardian agent team to continuously monitor agent activity and prevent dangerous behaviors before they occur. Perception has received positive feedback from preview customers, including KPMG, Nationwide Building Society, Northern Trust, and Salentis. More broadly, the company is helping customers secure and govern AI usage across the entire enterprise. To date, customers have used Microsoft Purview to audit over 7.6 billion agent activities, a fivefold increase quarter-over-quarter. Underpinning all of this is infrastructure. The company is building fungible compute pools to support growing backlog demand, dynamically allocating capacity to the highest-value opportunities in computing, data, Foundry, and Copilot. Demand for accelerated growth led the company to add 24 new data centers across five continents this quarter and accelerate capacity ramp-up. In the largest regions, which constitute the bulk of GPU deployments, the "doctor lifetime" (i.e., delivery cycle) for the new GB300 units shortened by approximately 20% quarter-over-quarter. Meanwhile, the company extracts more value from existing infrastructure by optimizing data center design, chip systems, software, and models. For example, throughput for Copilot workloads increased by over 50% quarter-over-quarter. The company continues to expand its compute pool with the latest innovations from NVIDIA, AMD, and its proprietary Maia systems, having installed the first batch of NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs with great enthusiasm. Maia 200 has achieved up to 1.7 times higher token output per watt in Copilot AI experiences and teams, and Maia 300 will further drive gains, improving token output per watt by 40% compared to leading GPU systems. Growth extends beyond GPUs. The company’s self-developed cloud-native Cobalt CPU continues to see strong adoption, improving price-performance for general cloud workloads. Overall Azure growth remains broad-based across enterprise and SMB customers, as well as core cloud services and AI infrastructure. Finally, regarding devices and consumer business, in Windows, the company is executing its vision of "bringing hybrid intelligence to every desk and every home, making every PC a secure agent container." As more powerful models run locally, there is an opportunity to make intelligence effectively unmetered. The company is collaborating with a broader hardware ecosystem to bring these capabilities to new PCs based on the AMD Ryzen AI 400 series, Intel Core Ultra Series 3, and Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 series. Earlier this month, the company also announced new PCs featuring NVIDIA RTX Spark and DGX Station for Windows. With these new devices, users can run last year’s frontier models on laptops and last quarter’s models on desktops. The company integrates Windows with Agent 365, enabling agents to operate within secure boundaries on devices. The company introduced Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC)—a policy-driven execution layer that governs and contains agents on Windows and other platforms, integrating with Agent 365 for governance and observability. Agents such as OpenAI Codex, Anthropic Claude Code, and Meta Muse are adopting MXC, with customers like Meta beginning to deploy them in their enterprise environments. In Search and Advertising, Bing and Edge again gained share. On LinkedIn, engagement among its 1.4 billion members continued to deepen, with time spent viewing feed content up 15% year over year. In Gaming, the company focuses on delivering high-quality games across consoles, PC, mobile, and cloud platforms chosen by players. Minecraft delivered a record quarter, with both engagement and revenue reaching all-time highs; World of Warcraft hosted the largest test in the series’ history. The company enters the holiday season with its strongest first-party lineup in years, including Modern Warfare IV, released last week to the best critical reception for the Call of Duty franchise in over a decade, and Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6), launching on Xbox next month. In summary, based on the demand we are seeing, the strength of our products, and the efficiency driven by our cross-technology stack, management has never been more confident in the long-term return on investment. Morgan Stanley Analyst Adam Wood: Drivers of AI Infrastructure Returns Question: With capital expenditures below expectations and better quarter-over-quarter cloud gross margin performance, as new AI capacity comes online, what will be the more critical driver of returns in the coming years: improvements in utilization rates and unit costs within the year, or the ability to monetize each workload across more layers atop Fabric, Foundry, and Copilot? Answer (Satya Nadella): It involves all of the above factors. Our strategy is to build a pool of compute that is as efficient and interchangeable as possible—this encompasses the entire physical aspect of data center construction, the operational rigor of bringing capacity online, and how optimized workloads run on this infrastructure. Once this is achieved, allocation simply follows demand signals. This is evident even under the new segment reporting structure: the stateful database underlying Copilot is Work IQ, which is utilized in Foundry—where customers build multi-agent systems for supply chains spanning unstructured and structured data, naturally using PostgreSQL databases within Azure. Furthermore, all agent work is registered in Agent 365, with security managed by Perception. Thus, we view these as part of the same infrastructure, merely reported under different product forms. The core question is where profit and leverage originate—not from any single link, but from every link, and when we connect them, the benefits compound. Answer (Amy Hood): Apologies, Adam, if I missed the first part of the question, I have at least addressed the latter part. UBS Group Analyst Karl Keirstedt: Drivers of the 49%-50% Azure Growth Guidance Question: Could you provide a further breakdown of one of the key metrics from this conference—the 49% to 50% growth guidance for Azure in December at constant currency? One can imagine many variables: capacity coming online, allocation to third-party customers, and potentially the strength of OpenAI. However, given the robustness of this figure, please discuss some of the key drivers. Answer (Amy Hood): Let’s start with the first fiscal quarter, as it helps inform projections for the second quarter and beyond, which also relates to Adam’s question. In Q1, our engineering team delivered exceptional work in improving efficiency at the platform layer. This refers not only to GPU efficiency but to efficiency across every layer: how applications utilize the platform, how Foundry utilizes the platform, and the Azure platform itself. These efficiency gains accumulate incrementally each week; some approaches succeed while others do not, requiring continuous investment. Consequently, their impact within a single quarter may not be precisely predictable. Q1 performance was strong, partly reflected in the company’s ability to allocate more capacity to Foundry during the quarter. This is positive because, as previously mentioned, demand continues to exceed supply. Whenever the engineering team delivers such efficiencies, we strive to apply them to Foundry, as Satya noted, because this is critical for customers broadly building new stacks. Secondly, token pricing introduces some volatility. Token pricing exceeded expectations this quarter—the healthy margins driven by high-quality models indeed benefited the company, as seen in Q1. Furthermore, in Q1 data, the aforementioned efficiencies applied not only to the GPU compute pool. People may have underestimated the integrated workloads involving GPUs, CPUs, storage, and memory cited in Satya’s examples—it encompasses all components. Thus, the company was also able to create additional capacity within existing compute pools, translating into results relatively quickly in Q1. In Q2, these efficiency gains will continue, and we need to uncover further efficiencies. We are confident in this regard, as the team’s Q1 work is expected to carry over into Q2, and such efforts are needed to provide support, since some supply originally anticipated for Q2 has been deferred to the second half of the year. Additionally, there is uncertainty regarding token pricing within the quarter. Overall, we are satisfied with the observed efficiency gains and are comfortable providing guidance based on them; however, other aspects remain difficult to predict. Bernstein Analyst Mark Moerdler: Drivers of Azure AI Growth Question: Regarding the drivers behind Azure AI’s strength, is it primarily enterprise customers or general digital-native/AI-native customers? As inference volumes begin to scale and Microsoft becomes the preferred choice for enterprises, how should we view the proportion of current enterprise workloads within the total workload mix? Also, what are the drivers behind the strong growth of Azure AI platform products—is it again driven by enterprises or digital-native customers (clearly a mix, but details highlighting enterprise scaling would be more valuable)? Answer (Satya Nadella): Last week in Europe, the quality of agent systems we observed was impressive, and they are being widely deployed. For example, a fully automated, contactless agent system on a delivery platform covers automatic order placement and dispute management for transaction vouchers. Rolls-Royce has deployed a system to manage its maintenance—its jet engines involve 30,000 parts, representing a highly complex supply chain, with planning, execution, and inventory management systems all built on Foundry and implemented as agents. Raiffeisen Bank International (RBI) in Austria showcased more than 20 end-to-end business processes, whether for credit approval or other functions, all optimized for better completion. The breadth, quality, and multi-model nature of these deployments are notable—they start with frontier models, and in Unilever’s case, even directly use MAI models trained on company traces. The maturity level in model optimization, workload optimization, and token optimization is encouraging. Breadth is beginning to unfold. Ultimately, enterprise workloads feel akin to how enterprises used to build database applications; this pattern is recurring in the AI domain today. In fact, certain "novelty-chasing" elements are fading, as enterprises focus more on whether they can build a system, own weights, manage costs, ensure reliability, and address security. Thus, the movement toward enterprise breadth is underway. However, like all things, enterprise business is not quarterly but operates on a decade-long horizon—this is what the company is waiting for, rather than having just four customers purchasing large amounts of capacity to show growth for a few quarters (which does not constitute a sustainable business). The company pursues breadth. We are well-positioned in terms of breadth among large customers and remain open to business: if the price is right, we can sell some capacity; otherwise, we will patiently build a broad-based business. Goldman Sachs Analyst Gabriela Borges: Token Mix and Evolution of Token Value Question: On the topic of "breadth," management mentioned that MAI can now match leading models within three to six months of their release, while OpenAI accounted for 11% of total revenue this quarter. Could you step back and share your latest thinking on how the token mix and token value will evolve among frontier models, MAI, and proprietary AI strategies of some mature enterprise customers? Answer (Satya Nadella): You can understand the toolbox for any workload through three lenses. First, when new models are released with superior performance, customers can evaluate them against their desired outcomes and adopt them—as happened with some OpenAI models last quarter. They were excellent, and we are excited about OpenAI’s progress on Astra and its future potential, seeing strong demand. Second, customers then ask: Can we simultaneously use multiple frontier models, given their significant price differences? In fact, in the true benchmark provided by Artificial Analysis this morning—using our Fusion coding agent—we ranked second or third, which is very encouraging: achieving frontier performance, a 45% speed increase, and a 75% price reduction is compelling. For coding agent users, the hope is that Anthropic and OpenAI compete for every task, not just once per quarter, which is precisely the value of routing and Fusion’s automatic routing. Third, and importantly, many customers—such as Unilever—have their own systems. Even after completing substantial work with frontier models, they ultimately wish to train their own models, which could be open-weight models or, as in this case, MAI models. Therefore, all these should be available options, and customers will choose based on pricing and demand. There is a temporal dimension to this: it is not about starting somewhere and staying there indefinitely. One might start with frontier models, then shift to open-weight models or MAI models, and return to frontier models for a few months upon the next release—workloads are dynamic in this way. Thus, across Foundry, Fabric, Copilot, and GitHub Copilot, we aim to build a model system that continuously delivers value to customers, rather than locking them into a single option. Jefferies Analyst Brent Thill: Maintaining 50% Revenue Growth and 50% Operating Margin Question: Azure’s growth rate is approaching 50%, and its operating margin is also nearing 50%. The market often asks: How can this growth be sustained while maintaining both top-line growth and bottom-line margins at the 50% level? Please discuss the ongoing operational improvements being pursued to sustain high bottom-line performance. Answer (Amy Hood): First, the best solution is revenue growth. Therefore, we should always start from the top of the income statement and work our way down—although many people assume companies work from the bottom up. The core of what the company does, which runs through all our commentary, is adjusting our segment structure because the way we deliver products and services is changing—we are delivering new, more integrated products with higher value. As top-line revenue accelerates, it naturally contributes positively to operating margins and gross profit dollars in a healthy manner. Second, the company is truly focused on efficiency. When people hear "efficiency," they often think of cost. While the results are related to cost, the true benefits of efficiency lie in stability, security, and reliability—delivering the highest quality units at the lowest cost, which is operational excellence. Therefore, on top of product quality (which performed very well last quarter), we layer continuous improvement at the operational level and a focus on operating expenses, ensuring they are directed toward building new capabilities or providing security and quality. The company has made very proactive choices to focus on these two areas, especially given their heightened importance in the current environment. When we achieve this while benefiting from a strong market with broad customer reach and global operations, we see good results. This was particularly evident this quarter: we delivered significant efficiency gains, enabling revenue growth without additional costs, which naturally flowed through to earnings. Management is satisfied with the elements supporting these figures—namely, our focus on the right levers. Stifel Analyst Brad Reback: Unlocking the M365 Consumption Model Question: When the company shifted GitHub from a per-seat model to a consumption model, it unlocked significant revenue growth. For core M365 customers, with the tools now in place on the consumption side, will the unlock speed be equally fast and require no sales effort, or will it take considerable effort to get these "meters" running? Answer (Satya Nadella): It will be faster on the coding side because the market is already accustomed to pay-as-you-go models. In fact, products like Fusion announced today at GitHub Universe offer a more attractive approach—customers purchase credits and aim to use them as efficiently as possible, which is exactly the promise of GitHub Copilot Fusion. The company is optimistic about this. Regarding Copilot itself, in a sense, with every model release, we are injecting more value into the subscription, effectively consolidating and promoting frontier capabilities. In many cases, this is funded by IT, as organizations seek to standardize deployment. At the same time, we retain pay-as-you-go or consumption meters for scenarios that require them. Both options are available, and we are working to help customers understand both and use them optimally, rather than over-purchasing one and falling into a trap of token maximization that benefits no one. We want customers to understand the value of subscriptions—they are continuously improving, not static—while also leveraging consumption meters. This represents a maturation in both sales execution and customer understanding. The company is satisfied with the progress, but there is still much work to be done. Answer (Amy Hood): This is also why the company is investing in frontier companies and aligning with the aforementioned changes in sales execution—both are indispensable. As Satya stated, we want customers to fully utilize their Copilot licenses while also understanding when consumption meters bring them value. Investments in the Frontier Deployment Engineers (FDE) organization or Frontier collaboration, as well as new initiatives within the Modern Work and Microsoft 365 sales teams, are all aimed at achieving this. As Satya noted, migration outside of coding will be slower, but we still see encouraging signs and remain positive. Bank of America Analyst Tal Liani: Capital Strategy Question: Regarding capital commitments and capital strategy, management mentioned in their statement that financing would be pursued if necessary in the future. Could you discuss the strategy among debt, equity, and other sources, and how you would finance if needed? Also, please confirm whether Copilot-related figures were disclosed this quarter. The company is satisfied with positive free cash flow and confident in the return on every dollar of capital expenditure, thus possessing ample options to engage financing markets when appropriate and attractive. Regarding the direct question—no specific Copilot figures were disclosed this quarter; we only discussed the momentum in revenue and usage.
